name: Virtual Camera and Lensing
title: Virtual Camera and Lensing
answer: Virtual camera and lensing covers the simulation of optical and mechanical camera properties inside synthetic and AI-generated video. This includes focal length, aperture, depth of field, sensor size, lens distortion, bokeh, and camera movement. The practice sits between traditional cinematography and generative video synthesis, giving creators control over framing and focus without a physical camera. It applies to fully generated scenes, real-time virtual production, and post-production compositing.

sections.body: Virtual camera and lensing covers the simulation of optical and mechanical camera properties inside synthetic and AI-generated video. This includes focal length, aperture, depth of field, sensor size, lens distortion, bokeh, and camera movement. The practice sits between traditional cinematography and generative video synthesis, giving creators control over framing and focus without a physical camera. It applies to fully generated scenes, real-time virtual production, and post-production compositing.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on GPU-based rendering and neural network inference. Video generation models are trained on large collections of footage paired with camera metadata, such as focal length and aperture. Real-time engines and compositing tools provide the interactive layer where virtual cameras are placed and animated. Some pipelines use neural radiance fields or 3D Gaussian splats to reconstruct a scene and then move a virtual camera through it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Camera parameters are encoded as conditioning inputs to a generative model, so a text or keyframe prompt can specify a 35mm lens at f/2.8 or a slow dolly move. Lens effects are produced either by physically based ray tracing or by learned optical models that approximate real glass. Camera paths can be generated from scripts, tracked from live action, or drawn by an operator. The output is reviewed in the same way as live-action footage, with attention to focus, parallax, and motion blur.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Synthetic footage made with virtual cameras can be difficult to distinguish from recorded video, which raises risks around fabricated events and non-consensual likenesses. Training data provenance and consent for people and locations remain open issues. Camera and lens metadata can serve as forensic evidence, but it is often stripped or absent in shared files. Rights to a particular lens look or camera move are not settled, and creators should document their sources and outputs.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Virtual camera and lensing is moving toward physically accurate lens simulation that includes real aberrations, breathing, and flare. Real-time control is improving, allowing directors to adjust focal length and aperture during a generated take. Automated camera direction from a script or storyboard is an active area of research. The likely result is a tighter link between generative video and established cinematography practice, with virtual cameras becoming a standard part of previsualization and final pixel work.
